question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
The Supreme Court
P. must remind the state to act constitutionally,
Q. lawfully and justly in every case across the
R. country, especially in sensitive matters involving
S. those who oppose the party in office with peaceful means
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. PQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly rearranged sentence reads: "The Supreme Court must remind the state to act constitutionally, lawfully and justly in every case across the country, especially in sensitive matters involving those who oppose the party in office with peaceful means."

• P logically follows the fixed opening "The Supreme Court" because it supplies the main verb of the sentence — "must remind the state to act constitutionally".

• Q follows P because "lawfully and justly" continues the list of adverbs begun by "constitutionally", and "in every case across the" sets up the noun that R begins with.

• R follows Q, completing "across the country" and introducing "especially in sensitive matters involving", which needs a subject — supplied by S.

• S closes the sentence with "those who oppose the party in office with peaceful means", the object of "involving".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: PQSR is incorrect because it places S before R, breaking the link between "across the" (end of Q) and "country" (start of R).

• Option 3: QPSR is incorrect because it starts with Q, which cannot logically follow "The Supreme Court" — the sentence would begin without a main verb.

• Option 4: QRSP is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3, and additionally disconnects P (which carries the main verb "must remind") from the opening phrase.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always locate the part that carries the main verb first — it usually attaches directly to any fixed opening or closing phrase.

• Look for grammatical "glue" — articles, prepositions, and conjunctions split across two parts (like "across the" / "country") — these pairs must always stay adjacent in the correct order.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
Give off gas bubbles
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Effervescent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Effervescent means giving off small bubbles of gas; fizzy. (गैस के बुलबुले छोड़ने वाला/उबलता हुआ)
◦ Example: She dropped a tablet into the glass and watched the effervescent water fizz.

• The word comes from the Latin effervescere, "to boil up, froth up", from ex- (out) + fervescere (to begin to boil).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Buoyant (उत्प्लावक/प्रफुल्लित): able to float, or cheerful and full of energy — not related to gas bubbles.

• Option 3: Flat (बेस्वाद/समतल): having lost its fizz, i.e. the opposite of giving off gas bubbles.

• Option 4: Effuse (फैलाना/निकलना): to pour out or emit (a liquid, light, or feeling) freely — close in spelling but wrong in meaning, as it does not specifically mean releasing gas bubbles.

NOTE

• Do not confuse effervescent (fizzy, giving off bubbles) with effusive (expressing feelings in an unrestrained way, e.g. "an effusive welcome").

• Other useful "one word for a group of words" science-based terms: volatile (evaporates easily), soluble (dissolves easily), combustible (catches fire easily).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
In black and white
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. In writing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "In black and white" means in writing or in print, so as to be official or beyond doubt. (लिखित रूप में)
◦ Example: Get the agreement in black and white before you start the work.

• The phrase refers to the black ink used to print or write on white paper, implying something documented and undeniable, unlike a verbal promise.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: In trouble (मुसीबत में): facing difficulty or a problem.

• Option 3: In suspense (उलझन/अनिश्चितता में): in a state of anxious uncertainty about what will happen.

• Option 4: In brief (संक्षेप में): in a few words; concisely.

NOTE

• Other idioms of authenticity/documentation often asked in SSC: "Straight from the horse's mouth" (from a reliable, direct source), "To take something at face value", and "On record" (officially stated).

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One who feeds on plants only
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Herbivorous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Herbivorous means feeding only on plants. (केवल शाकाहारी/वनस्पति खाने वाला)
◦ Example: Cows and deer are herbivorous animals.

• The word derives from Latin herba (plant/grass) + vorare (to devour).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Vermivorous (कृमिभक्षी): feeding on worms.

• Option 2: Carnivorous (मांसाहारी): feeding on the flesh of other animals.

• Option 3: Omnivorous (सर्वाहारी): feeding on both plants and animals.

NOTE

• Related "-vorous" one-word substitutions frequently asked in SSC: insectivorous (feeds on insects), piscivorous (feeds on fish), frugivorous (feeds on fruit), graminivorous (feeds on grass).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Dandy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Beautiful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Dandy, used informally as an adjective, means excellent, fine, or very good/smart-looking. (उत्तम/बांका)
◦ Example: That's a dandy little gadget you've got there.

• As a noun, a "dandy" is a man unduly concerned with looking stylish and elegant; by extension, the adjective use conveys something impressively fine or attractive, which among the given options is best matched by "Beautiful".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Cartel (गठजोड़): an association of manufacturers or suppliers to control prices — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 2: Disappointment (निराशा): sadness caused by the non-fulfilment of hopes — the opposite sense of "dandy".

• Option 3: Dud (बेकार वस्तु): something that fails to work; a worthless item — nearly opposite to "dandy".

NOTE

• Words for a stylish/well-dressed person often tested in SSC: fop, coxcomb, popinjay (all meaning a man overly concerned with his appearance).

• Do not confuse "dandy" (fine/stylish) with "dandruff" (flakes of dead skin on the scalp) — a common distractor in spelling-based sets.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Young
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Mature.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mature means fully developed physically or mentally; grown-up, which is the direct opposite of "Young" (having lived or existed for only a short time). (परिपक्व/प्रौढ़)
◦ Example: He behaved in a mature way despite the crisis, quite unlike his young, immature colleagues.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Limited (सीमित): restricted in amount or extent — unrelated to age.

• Option 2: Silly (मूर्खतापूर्ण): having or showing a lack of good sense — a trait, not an age-related opposite of "young".

• Option 4: Gravity (गंभीरता/गुरुत्वाकर्षण): seriousness, or the force that attracts bodies — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other common SSC antonym pairs around age/development: youthful × aged, juvenile × adult, fresh × stale, novice × veteran.

• "Mature" can also describe fruit (ripe) or a financial instrument (due for payment) — watch for context in reading comprehension.

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
The objective was to / dispose off a cargo of cotton which/ I had brought from Mumbai port.
option_2: I had brought from Mumbai port.
option_3: dispose off a cargo of cotton which
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. dispose off a cargo of cotton which.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "dispose off", which should be "dispose of".

• Rule: The verb "dispose", when meaning "to get rid of" or "to deal with finally", always takes the preposition "of", never "off". "Dispose off" is a very common but incorrect usage.
◦ Correct: dispose of a cargo of cotton.

• The corrected sentence reads: "The objective was to dispose of a cargo of cotton which I had brought from Mumbai port."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The objective was to" is grammatically correct — a standard infinitive construction.

• Option 2: "I had brought from Mumbai port." is correct — the past perfect "had brought" correctly shows an action completed before another past action (the disposal).

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect since an error does exist, in Option 3.

NOTE

• Commonly confused preposition pairs tested by SSC: dispose of (get rid of) vs dispose off (wrong usage); compare to (different things) vs compare with (similar things); differ from (things) vs differ with (opinion).

• "Dispose" without "of" changes meaning entirely: "to dispose troops" means to arrange/position them.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
This whole plot come under my uncle's jurisdiction.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. come under my.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the verb "come", which should be "comes".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A singular subject takes a singular verb. "This whole plot" is a singular subject (governed by the singular demonstrative "This"), so it must take the singular verb "comes", not "come".

• The corrected sentence reads: "This whole plot comes under my uncle's jurisdiction."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect since an error does exist.

• Option 2: "uncle's jurisdiction." is correct — the possessive apostrophe is properly used.

• Option 4: "This whole plot" is correct as a noun phrase in itself; the agreement error only becomes apparent with the verb in the next part, which is why the error is attributed to "come under my".

NOTE

• Singular subjects that are commonly mistaken for plural in SSC error-spotting: each, everyone, everybody, nobody, either, neither, the whole/entire + noun — all take a singular verb.

• Watch for a long subject noun phrase separating the subject from the verb — the error is often "hidden" a few words after the true subject.

question:
The given sentence is in active voice. Change the voice of the sentence. Select the correct option from the sentences given in options.
I know he will play his guitar.
option_1: His guitar will be played by him is something I know.
option_2: It is known to me that his guitar would be played by him.
option_3: It is known to me that his guitar will be played by him.
option_4: His guitar will be played by him is know to me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. It is known to me that his guitar will be played by him.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "I know he will play his guitar" has two clauses: the main clause "I know" (Simple Present Tense) and the subordinate clause "he will play his guitar" (Simple Future Tense).

• Rule — Passive of "I know that...": The main clause "I know" becomes "It is known to me".

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + be + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule to the subordinate clause: "he will play his guitar" → object "his guitar" becomes the subject, verb "play" (V1) becomes "played" (V3), giving "his guitar will be played by him".

• Joining both parts with "that": It is known to me that his guitar will be played by him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it awkwardly reverses the clause order and drops the connecting "that" structure, producing an ungrammatical sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "would be played" wrongly changes the tense of the subordinate clause from simple future to a conditional form; the tense of the subordinate clause must be preserved as simple future.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "is know to me" uses the base form "know" instead of the past participle "known", making it grammatically wrong.

NOTE

• When a sentence has the pattern "Subject + know/think/say/believe + that + clause", only the reported (subordinate) clause is usually converted to passive, while the reporting clause becomes an impersonal passive like "It is said/known/believed that...".

• Common impersonal-passive openers: It is said that..., It is believed that..., It is reported that..., It is expected that...

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Until you confess your crime, the abdomen would ______ to grow and grow until you could not breathe.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. continue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Continue means to keep happening or existing without stopping, which fits the sense of the abdomen growing without interruption "until you could not breathe".

• The phrase "continue to grow and grow" correctly conveys an ongoing, repeated, uninterrupted process, matching the idea of the growth persisting until confession.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: expire — to come to an end, or to die; the opposite sense of ongoing growth, so it does not fit.

• Option 2: desist — to stop doing something; this is the opposite of the intended meaning of continuous growth.

• Option 4: reckon — to think, calculate, or consider; does not fit the sense of the abdomen's physical growth continuing.

NOTE

• In fill-in-the-blank vocabulary questions, always check whether the surrounding context calls for a word of continuation (continue, persist, proceed) or cessation (desist, cease, halt) — "grow and grow" is a strong repetition signal pointing to continuation.

• Common confusable pair: desist (formal, to stop an action) vs resist (to withstand or oppose something).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Grudje.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Grudge", not "Grudje" — meaning a persistent feeling of ill will or resentment.

• Spelling key: G-R-U-D-G-E. The letters "d" and "g" appear consecutively before the final silent "e"; the incorrect option wrongly swaps this to "dj".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Block" is correctly spelt — a solid piece of hard material, or to obstruct.

• Option 3: "Flown" is correctly spelt — the past participle of "fly".

• Option 4: "Adhere" is correctly spelt — to stick firmly to a surface or, figuratively, to a plan or set of rules.

NOTE

• Words ending in a "-dge" sound are frequently misspelled by writing "dj" instead — practice similar words: badge, edge, judge, pledge, wedge, lodge.

• Always sound out silent-letter and consonant-cluster words carefully; SSC frequently tests such near-miss spellings (e.g. "Grudje" for "Grudge").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Bite the dust
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To die.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bite the dust" means to die, or more broadly, to fail or come to an end. (मर जाना)
◦ Example: Many soldiers bit the dust in that fierce battle.

• The phrase originates from the image of a person falling face-down onto the ground (dust) at the moment of death, especially in battle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To lose a fight (लड़ाई हारना): a related but narrower/related sense; the idiom's core meaning taught by SSC is "to die", not merely losing a contest.

• Option 2: To grieve over (शोक मनाना): to feel or express deep sorrow, unrelated to this idiom.

• Option 3: To hate (नफरत करना): to feel intense dislike, unrelated to this idiom.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to death frequently tested in SSC: "To kick the bucket" (to die), "To breathe one's last" (to die), "To pass away" (to die, polite form).

• "Bite the dust" is also used informally in modern usage to mean "to fail" or "to be defeated/eliminated" (e.g., "another start-up bites the dust"), but its primary, exam-tested meaning is "to die".

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.
(Neither of the two have cleared the) aptitude test.
option_1: Neither of two have cleared the
option_2: Neither of the two boys have cleared
option_4: Neither of the two has cleared the
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Neither of the two has cleared the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error in the original sentence is the verb "have", which should be "has".

• Rule — "Neither" as Subject: "Neither" (and "Either") is always treated as a singular pronoun, even when followed by "of the two/of them", and therefore takes a singular verb.
◦ Correct: Neither of the two has cleared the aptitude test.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Neither of two have cleared the" is incorrect — it drops the required article "the" before "two", and still retains the wrong plural verb "have".

• Option 2: "Neither of the two boys have cleared" is incorrect because it still uses the plural verb "have" with the singular subject "Neither", and additionally omits "the" before "aptitude test" causing incompleteness.

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect since the original sentence does contain a subject-verb agreement error.

NOTE

• Other singular-only pronouns frequently tested in SSC: each, everyone, everybody, someone, anybody, nobody, either, neither — all always take a singular verb regardless of what follows them.

• Do not confuse "neither...nor" (used for two alternatives, singular verb usually agrees with the nearer subject) with "none" (used for more than two, can take a singular or plural verb depending on context).

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
One who is against religion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Heretic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A Heretic is a person holding an opinion or belief contrary to accepted religious doctrine, i.e., one who goes against established religious teachings. (धर्म-विरोधी/पाखंडी)
◦ Example: The priest denounced him as a heretic for questioning the church's teachings.

• The word comes from Greek hairetikos, meaning "able to choose", referring to someone who chooses a belief contrary to the orthodox one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Poacher (अवैध शिकारी): one who hunts or fishes illegally on another's land or in violation of the law.

• Option 2: Lunatic (पागल): a person who is mentally ill; used informally for a foolish or reckless person.

• Option 3: Bandit (डाकू): a robber or outlaw, typically one of an armed gang.

NOTE

• Related religion-based one-word substitutions asked in SSC: atheist (one who does not believe in the existence of God), agnostic (one who believes nothing can be known about the existence of God), theist (one who believes in the existence of God), iconoclast (one who attacks cherished beliefs/traditions).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Habitat
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Niche.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Habitat means the natural home or environment of an animal, plant, or other organism. (प्राकृतिक आवास)
◦ Example: The rainforest is the natural habitat of many rare species.

• Niche, in an ecological sense, means the specific environment/position that is suited to a particular organism, making it the closest synonym among the given options. (उपयुक्त स्थान/आवास)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Motion (गति): the action or process of moving — unrelated to habitat.

• Option 2: Clothed (वस्त्र पहने हुए): wearing clothes — unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: Bent (झुका हुआ/रुझान): curved, or a natural inclination/liking — unrelated to habitat.

NOTE

• Related environment/ecology vocabulary tested by SSC: ecosystem (a biological community and its environment), terrain (a stretch of land), habitation (the state of living in a place or a settlement).

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
CAJOLE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. PERSUADE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cajole means to persuade someone to do something by sustained coaxing or flattery. (चापलूसी से मनाना)
◦ Example: She cajoled her brother into lending her the car.

• Among the given options, "Persuade" (to induce someone to do something through reasoning or argument) is the closest in meaning, since both involve getting someone to agree or comply, though cajole specifically implies flattery/coaxing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: DISSUADE (हतोत्साहित करना): to persuade someone NOT to do something — nearly the opposite of cajole.

• Option 3: BULLY (धमकाना): to use force or threats to intimidate someone — opposite in method (coercion, not flattery).

• Option 4: DISENCHANT (मोहभंग करना): to cause someone to become disillusioned — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "cajole" frequently tested in SSC: coax, wheedle, entice, flatter.

• Do not confuse cajole (to coax with flattery) with console (to comfort someone in distress) — a common distractor pair.

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
Exclusive command or possession
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Monopoly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Monopoly means the exclusive possession or control of the supply of or trade in a commodity or service, i.e., exclusive command or possession of something. (एकाधिकार)
◦ Example: The company held a monopoly over the region's electricity supply.

• The word derives from Greek monos (single) + polein (to sell).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Sanctum (पवित्र स्थान): a sacred or private place.

• Option 3: Hypergamy (उच्च वर्ग में विवाह): marriage to a person of a superior caste or class.

• Option 4: Parvenu (नवधनाढ्य): a person of obscure origin who has recently gained wealth or power.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions on economic control asked in SSC: oligopoly (control by a small number of sellers), monopsony (a market with a single buyer), cartel (an association of producers to control prices).

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: Peel and pit avocados and cut into slice
option_2: Peel and pit avacados and cut into slice.
option_3: Peal and pitt avocados and cut into slise.
option_4: Peale and pit avocados and cut into slise.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Peel and pit avocados and cut into slice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Every word in Option 1 — "Peel", "pit", "avocados", "cut", "into", "slice" — is spelt correctly.

• Checking each word: Peel (not "Peal"/"Peale"), pit (not "pitt"), avocados (not "avacados"), slice (not "slise").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Peel and pit avacados and cut into slice." is incorrect because "avacados" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "avocados".

• Option 3: "Peal and pitt avocados and cut into slise." is incorrect because "Peal" (should be "Peel"), "pitt" (should be "pit") and "slise" (should be "slice") are all misspelt.

• Option 4: "Peale and pit avocados and cut into slise." is incorrect because "Peale" (should be "Peel") and "slise" (should be "slice") are misspelt.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Peel" (to remove the outer skin) with "Peal" (a loud ringing of bells, or a burst of sound, e.g. "a peal of thunder") — a classic homophone trap in SSC spelling questions.

• Practice similarly tricky food-related spellings: avocado, broccoli, cauliflower, vegetable, restaurant.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. actually move so slowly that algae grows on their fur and
Q. the forest from predators like nocturnal cats and harpy eagles
R. this can give sloths a green colour that helps them hide in
S. sloths live in tropical forests in South and Central America, and they
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. SPRQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly rearranged sentence reads: "Sloths live in tropical forests in South and Central America, and they actually move so slowly that algae grows on their fur and this can give sloths a green colour that helps them hide in the forest from predators like nocturnal cats and harpy eagles."

• S is the natural opening, introducing the subject "sloths" and their habitat.

• P follows S, continuing with "they actually move so slowly that algae grows on their fur", describing the sloths' behaviour.

• R follows P, since the algae growth described in P is what "can give sloths a green colour that helps them hide in".

• Q closes the sentence, completing "hide in the forest from predators like nocturnal cats and harpy eagles".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: PSQR is incorrect because it starts with P, which cannot logically open the sentence without a subject having first been introduced ("sloths").

• Option 2: RQPS is incorrect for the same reason — R refers to "this" (the algae effect) before it has been introduced.

• Option 4: SRQP is incorrect because R ("this can give sloths a green colour") cannot directly follow S, since "this" has no antecedent (the algae growth) until P is stated.

NOTE

• In descriptive para-jumbles, track pronouns like "this", "it", "they" — such a pronoun must always come after the noun/idea it refers to.

• Look for cause-effect chains (behaviour → result) as one common structural pattern used to build these sentences.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
The coach said to the student, “When will you come for practice?”
option_1: The coach asked the student when he will come for practice.
option_2: The coach asked the student when he would came for practice.
option_3: The coach asked the student when he would come for practice.
option_4: The coach asked the student when would he come for practice.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The coach asked the student when he would come for practice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct sentence is a Wh-question (interrogative sentence) in the Simple Future Tense.

• Rule — Reporting Verb: For a question, "said to" changes to "asked" in indirect speech.

• Rule — Wh-Questions: The question word ("when") is retained as a connector; the sentence structure is changed back to assertive (Subject + Verb) order, and the question mark is removed.

• Rule — Tense Change: Since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, the future tense auxiliary "will" shifts back to "would"; the pronoun "you" changes to "he" to refer to the student.

• Applying these rules: "When will you come" → "when he would come", giving: The coach asked the student when he would come for practice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will" is not backshifted to "would", which is required since the reporting verb is in the past tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "would came" wrongly uses the past form "came" after the modal "would"; a modal must always be followed by the base form of the verb, i.e. "come".

• Option 4 is incorrect because it retains the question word order ("would he come") instead of converting it to the assertive order ("he would come") required in indirect speech.

NOTE

• Common tense backshifts in narration: will → would, can → could, may → might, is/am/are → was/were, has/have → had.

• In indirect Wh-questions, always remember: no question mark, no inversion, question word retained as a connector.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A recent study that (1) ________ people's brains at different points in their work day (2) ________ high-demand tasks which require intense, constant concentration can lead to build-up of a (3) ________ toxic chemical called glutamate. Normally used to (4) ________ signals from nerve cells, in large quantities glutamate alters the (5) ________ of a brain region involved in planning and decision making, the lateral prefrontal cortex (lPFC).

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. scanned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "A recent study that scanned people's brains at different points in their work day...".

• Scanned fits perfectly because studies examining brain activity typically use imaging technology (like fMRI) to scan the brain — i.e., to examine it systematically, usually with a medical device.

• This matches the overall context of a neuroscience study observing brain activity at different times of the workday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: buzzed — means made a low humming sound; it does not fit the sense of a scientific study examining brains.

• Option 2: illuminated — means lit up or made clear; while studies can "illuminate" a topic figuratively, it does not fit the literal description of examining brains with a device.

• Option 4: answered — means responded to; brains cannot be grammatically "answered" by a study in this context.

NOTE

• In cloze passages about scientific/medical studies, watch for collocations like "scan the brain", "conduct a study", "monitor activity" — these are commonly tested word-context pairings.

• Related vocabulary: imaging (creating a visual representation, as with MRI), probe (to investigate thoroughly).

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. found.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...at different points in their work day found high-demand tasks which require intense, constant concentration can lead to build-up of a...toxic chemical...", meaning the study found (discovered/concluded) that high-demand tasks lead to this build-up.

• Rule: The main verb of the sentence (describing what the study did, and reported as a completed research finding) must be in the simple past tense, matching the tense used throughout the rest of the passage ("A recent study that scanned..."). The correct simple past form of "find" is "found".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: founded — means "established" (e.g. founded a company); it is a different verb altogether (from "found/establish", not the past tense of "find"), and does not fit the meaning of discovering something through research.

• Option 3: find — is the base/present form, inconsistent with the simple past tense used consistently elsewhere in the passage ("scanned").

• Option 4: had founded — uses the past perfect of the wrong verb ("found" a company), which is both tense-inconsistent and meaning-inconsistent with the passage.

NOTE

• A very common SSC trap is confusing "found" (past tense of "find", to discover) with "founded" (past tense of "found", to establish/set up) — they are two entirely different base verbs.

• Maintain tense consistency across a cloze passage: once the passage establishes a past-tense narrative ("scanned"), subsequent main verbs describing the same timeline should also be in the simple past.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. potentially.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...can lead to build-up of a potentially toxic chemical called glutamate."

• Potentially means "possibly, as a capability that may or may not be realised", which is the appropriate qualifier here — glutamate is not toxic in all situations, but has the potential to become harmful under certain conditions (as the passage goes on to describe with "large quantities").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: utterly — means "completely, totally"; this would wrongly suggest the chemical is always completely toxic, contradicting the passage's later point that it only becomes harmful in "large quantities".

• Option 3: perpetually — means "continuing forever/constantly"; does not fit, as the chemical's harmful effect is conditional, not continuous.

• Option 4: grandly — means "in an impressive or grand manner"; does not make sense when describing a chemical's toxicity.

NOTE

• "Potentially" is a very common cloze-test word used before adjectives describing a possible-but-not-certain risk (e.g., "potentially dangerous", "potentially harmful", "potentially fatal").

• Distinguish degree adverbs: potentially (possibly), utterly/completely (totally), perpetually (always/continuously) — SSC often tests the correct one based on the certainty implied by the surrounding sentence.

NOTE
